# A hybrid agent: Jev decides, the LLM reasons {#sec-ch17}

::: {.epigraph by="Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776"}
The greatest improvement in the productive powers of labour … seem to have been the effects of the division of labour.
:::

Chapter 7's agent read an alert, chose evidence, decided whether it had enough, reached a verdict and acted. More than half its steps were small decisions. This chapter rebuilds it as a **hybrid**: a decision model makes every decision, and the LLM writes only what a person will read. Then we race it against an agent where the LLM does everything.

But first, a bug. It was there from the start, never caused a crash, and I found it only through a habit this chapter will teach you.

::: {.goals}
- Design an agent where typed decisions drive the loop and an LLM writes only for people.
- Read an agent's trace step by step, as a timeline and as an audit log.
- Find a decision step that's wrong without any error, by counting how often it gives each answer.
- Compare a hybrid agent with an all-LLM one on time, cost, review load and threats missed.
- Know which work to leave as a decision, and which to just do.
:::

## The shape of the hybrid

![The hybrid agent. A cheap lookup always runs first. Jev decides which other evidence to collect, then answers the three verdict questions together. Chapter 14's policy turns the verdict into an action, and the LLM writes a case note or urgent message only when a person will read it.](/figures/ch24/architecture.pdf){#fig-architecture-17}

In @fig-architecture-17, green boxes are typed questions to the decision model, blue boxes are tools that read something, and the policy is ordinary code. The LLM (orange) appears once, at the end, and only where a person is waiting to read.

Every run leaves a **trace**: a step-by-step record of what was observed, what each decision said with what probability, and which threshold it crossed. It's a debugging tool, an audit log and an explanation in one. When someone asks next month why an alert was closed, you read the trace.

## The bug that didn't crash

When I first ran the agent over the live week, everything looked fine: actions spread across the three zones, every answer parsed, no errors. Then I ran a check worth running on every decision step of every agent: *count its answers*.

![How often the first version of the agent chose each option at its "which evidence next?" step, across 700 live alerts. It never once chose threat intel.](/figures/ch24/never-picked.pdf){#fig-never-picked}

Across {{< num ch24 n int >}} alerts, the "which evidence next?" decision chose host history, the policy lookup and "none" about equally often. It never chose threat intel. Not once (@fig-never-picked).

So the verdict was always reached without the most useful fact about an alert, and the model used a default value instead. The ranking got worse: AUC {{< num ch24 v1_auc f3 >}}, against the {{< num ch24 v2_auc f3 >}} it reaches with threat intel. And about {{< num ch24 v1_closed_threats_day f1 >}} real threats a day were auto-closed.

![The same agent before and after one change: always fetching threat intel. Real threats auto-closed per day fell by more than half, and the verdict's ranking recovered.](/figures/ch24/fix.pdf){#fig-fix}

Careful about what this shows: the stand-in's choices come from simple word matching, so I can't say real Jev would make this mistake. But *any* decision step, answered by any model, can fail this way, and nothing downstream will complain. Typed answers always have the right format. The right format isn't the right answer.

::: {.keyidea}
Count every decision step's answers: an option never or always chosen is a warning, even without a crash.
:::

The fix wasn't a better prompt or a better model. It was a design change. A threat-intel lookup takes a fraction of a second and costs nothing. Deciding *whether* to look it up costs about as much as just looking.

::: {.keyidea}
When looking is cheaper than deciding whether to look, don't decide. Just look.
:::

## Comparing with the all-LLM agent

The all-LLM agent runs the same loop, tools and thresholds; only who decides changes. Every decision is an LLM call returning JSON, and the verdict uses the LLM's stated confidence. A broken answer goes to review.

![One alert's trace as a timeline, for each agent. Plain blue steps observe, striped green steps decide, dotted orange steps write, cross-hatched grey steps act. The hybrid's decisions are very thin bars; the all-LLM agent's decisions take most of its time.](/figures/ch24/trace.pdf){#fig-trace}

@fig-trace shows the difference on a single alert, and it's mostly the width of the green, striped decide bars. Across the sample, the hybrid took {{< num ch24 v2_seconds f1 >}} seconds per alert. The all-LLM agent took {{< num ch24 llm_seconds f1 >}}, about {{< num ch24 speedup int >}} times as long.

![Four measures for the two agents on the same 700 live alerts, scaled to a day. The LLM's stated confidences sent far more alerts to review than the queue can take, so more real threats were never seen by a person.](/figures/ch24/compare.pdf){#fig-compare-17}

The bigger difference is the review queue (@fig-compare-17). The all-LLM agent sent about {{< num ch24 llm_reviews_day int >}} alerts a day to review, against a capacity of 240. Its stated confidences cluster at a few round values, so the thresholds have almost nothing to separate, and most alerts land in the middle. The hybrid sent {{< num ch24 v2_reviews_day int >}}.

A queue at twice its capacity doesn't get worked twice as hard; the extra alerts just aren't seen, and nobody chooses which. Counting threats auto-closed *and* threats never reached in the queue, the hybrid let about {{< num ch24 v2_missed_day int >}} a day go unseen; the all-LLM agent, about {{< num ch24 llm_missed_day int >}}. Simulated cost: about \${{< num ch24 hybrid_cost_1000 f2 >}} per thousand alerts for the hybrid, mostly for the LLM writing case notes. For the all-LLM agent it's \${{< num ch24 llm_cost_1000 f2 >}}.

## Where the time goes

![Share of each agent's total time spent on each kind of step. In the hybrid, the largest share is the LLM writing for people. In the all-LLM agent, most of the time goes on deciding.](/figures/ch24/labour.pdf){#fig-labour}

@fig-labour is the most revealing chart. The all-LLM agent spends most of its time deciding. The hybrid spends its largest share *writing*: notes and messages a person will read. That's where an LLM's time belongs. The hybrid doesn't use less LLM because LLMs are bad; it uses the LLM where it's best.

::: {.keyidea}
Use the LLM for the work only an LLM can do.
:::

::: {.breaks}
Everything here is synthetic, timings included, and the accuracy gap between the agents is partly built into the stand-ins. Treat the speed, the queue and the design lessons as the findings, not the quality of the verdicts. And the bug shows a hybrid has its own failure mode: a decision step that's wrong without any error. Watching each step's answers isn't optional.
:::

::: {.threshold}
The hybrid agent's "which evidence next?" step can choose "none" to stop collecting evidence. Each extra lookup costs about 0.4 seconds and nothing else. Stopping too early, as the first version showed, can cost a missed threat. If you had to set a rule for when the agent may stop, what would it be? Would you let a probability decide it?

(One reasonable rule: never stop before the lookups that are cheap and always useful, like threat intel. Let the model decide only among the costly ones. Then check the rule like any other decision. Count how often "none" is chosen, and look at what it cost on the alerts where it was chosen.)
:::

Donald Knuth warned programmers not to optimise before measuring [@knuth1974]. The first version did exactly that: it made "should we look this up?" a clever decision, when simply looking was cheaper. Measure first, then decide what's worth deciding.

::: {.exercises}
1. You add a new evidence tool ("check the user's recent password resets"). Which rules from this chapter decide whether it should be a decision or a step that always runs?
2. Describe a daily check that would flag any decision step whose answers are suspiciously one-sided.
:::
